title: Quantitative Aptitude
description: Master the mathematical concepts required to solve placement aptitude problems quickly and accurately.

modules.title: Number Fundamentals
modules.description: Core number concepts and divisibility.

lessons.title: Number System
lessons.description: Introduction to the foundation of mathematics.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: A number system is a method of representing numbers mathematically using a set of digits or symbols.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Almost every quantitative problem starts with a solid understanding of basic number properties.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Numbers are divided into Real and Imaginary. Real numbers branch into Rational and Irrinal. Further classification gives Integers, Whole numbers, and Natural numbers.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Identify the category of a given number by checking if it can be represented as p/q (Rational) or if it has fractional parts.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: Is -5 a natural number? No, natural numbers start from 1. It is an integer.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Representing repeating decimals as fractions: 0.333... = 1/3.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Confusing whole numbers with natural numbers (0 is whole but not natural).

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Always check constraints in questions: if 'x is a positive integer', x cannot be 0.

sections.question: Which of the following is not a rational number?
sections.explanation: sqrt(2) cannot be written as a simple fraction, making it irrational.

lessons.title: Types of Numbers
lessons.description: Prime, composite, even, and odd numbers.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Numbers are classified by their divisibility properties.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Direct questions on prime numbers are very common in TCS and Infosys exams.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Even numbers are divisible by 2. Odd are not. Prime numbers have exactly two distinct factors (1 and itself). Composite numbers have more than two factors.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: To check if N is prime, you only need to check for divisibility by prime numbers up to sqrt(N).

sections.title: Example
sections.content: Is 91 a prime number? sqrt(91) is ~9.5. Primes to check: 2, 3, 5, 7. 91 is divisible by 7 (7*13=91). So, it's composite.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: 1 is neither prime nor composite. 2 is the only even prime number.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Assuming 1 is a prime number.
Assuming all odd numbers are prime (e.g., 9, 15).

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Memorize prime numbers up to 100 to save crucial seconds.

sections.question: How many prime numbers exist between 1 and 20?

lessons.title: Divisibility Rules
lessons.description: Quick checks for divisibility without full division.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Divisibility rules are shortcuts to determine if an integer is exactly divisible by another.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: These rules are essential for simplifying fractions and solving LCM/HCF questions rapidly.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content:
Rule of 3: Sum of digits is divisible by 3.
Rule of 4: Last 2 digits are divisible by 4.
Rule of 9: Sum of digits is divisible by 9.
Rule of 11: Difference between sum of odd-place digits and even-place digits is 0 or multiple of 11.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Add the digits or check specific positions depending on the rule.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: Is 3456 divisible by 9? Sum = 3+4+5+6 = 18. Since 18 is divisible by 9, 3456 is too.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Rule of 8: check if the last 3 digits are divisible by 8.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Adding digits for rule of 4 instead of looking at the last two digits.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: If a number is divisible by both 2 and 3, it is automatically divisible by 6.

sections.question: Which of the following numbers is divisible by 11?
sections.explanation: For 1331: Sum of odd places (1+3=4). Sum of even places (3+1=4). 4 - 4 = 0.

lessons.title: Factors and Multiples
lessons.description: Understanding the building blocks of numbers.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: A factor divides a number exactly. A multiple is formed by multiplying the number by an integer.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Forms the basis for LCM, HCF, and prime factorization questions.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Every number is a factor and multiple of itself. Number of factors can be found using prime factorization: if N = p^a * q^b, total factors = (a+1)(b+1).

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: To find total factors, prime factorize the number, add 1 to each exponent, and multiply them.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: If total factors is an odd number, the number is a perfect square.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Confusing factors with multiples (factors are smaller/equal, multiples are larger/equal).

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Finding the number of factors is much faster using prime factorization than counting manually.

sections.question: How many factors does the number 24 have?

lessons.title: LCM and HCF
lessons.description: Least Common Multiple and Highest Common Factor.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: LCM is the smallest common multiple of two or more numbers. HCF is the largest common divisor.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Almost guaranteed to appear in placement tests, especially in word problems involving cyclical events.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: LCM * HCF = Product of two numbers. For fractions, LCM = LCM of numerators / HCF of denominators.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Use the prime factorization method or division method to find LCM/HCF.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: If a problem asks for the 'minimum' time they meet again, it's LCM. If it asks to divide into 'largest' equal segments, it's HCF.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Using LCM logic when the question implies HCF.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: For circular track problems where people run at different speeds, finding when they meet at the start is an LCM of time problem.

sections.question: The HCF of two numbers is 8 and their product is 384. What is their LCM?
sections.explanation: LCM * HCF = Product. LCM * 8 = 384 -> LCM = 384/8 = 48.

modules.title: Arithmetic
modules.description: Percentages, profit/loss, and ratio concepts.

lessons.title: Percentages
lessons.description: Calculating parts per hundred.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Percentage means 'out of 100'. It is a fraction with a denominator of 100.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Percentages form the basis of Profit/Loss, SI/CI, and Data Interpretation.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: x% of y = (x/100) * y. Successive percentage change: A + B + (A*B/100).

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Always identify the 'base' value. 'A is what percent of B' = (A/B)*100.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: If salary increases by 20% then decreases by 20%: +20 - 20 - (20*20/100) = -4% (a 4% decrease).

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Learn standard fraction to percentage conversions: 1/3 = 33.33%, 1/6 = 16.66%, 1/8 = 12.5%.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Applying successive changes by simply adding them (20% up then 20% down is NOT 0%).

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Whenever a value increases by x% and then decreases by x%, there is always a net decrease of (x^2/100)%.

sections.question: A number is increased by 10% and then decreased by 10%. What is the net change?
sections.explanation: Successive change formula: +10 - 10 - (10*10)/100 = -1%. A 1% decrease.

lessons.title: Profit and Loss
lessons.description: Calculating business transactions.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Profit occurs when Selling Price (SP) > Cost Price (CP). Loss occurs when CP > SP.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: A fundamental concept tested heavily by TCS and Cognizant.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Profit % = (Profit/CP) * 100. Loss % = (Loss/CP) * 100. Markup and Discount are calculated on CP and MRP respectively.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Calculate everything relative to the Cost Price unless explicitly stated otherwise.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: If an article is sold at a loss of 20%, SP = 0.8 * CP.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Calculating Profit/Loss percentage on Selling Price instead of Cost Price.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Discount is ALWAYS calculated on the Marked Price (MRP), never on the Cost Price.

sections.question: If an item is bought for $40 and sold for $50, what is the profit percentage?

lessons.title: Ratio and Proportion
lessons.description: Comparing quantities and scaling.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: A ratio compares values. A proportion is an equation stating that two ratios are equal.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Used in mixtures, partnership, and age-related problems.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: If A:B = c:d, then A/B = c/d. If a:b and b:c are given, multiply to find a:b:c.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Use a common multiplier (x) for ratio problems.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: Divide 100 in ratio 2:3. Let parts be 2x and 3x. 5x = 100, x = 20. Parts are 40 and 60.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: To combine A:B = 2:3 and B:C = 4:5. Make B equal: A:B = 8:12, B:C = 12:15. So A:B:C = 8:12:15.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Adding ratios directly across different bases.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: In mixture problems, always track the quantity that remains constant.

sections.question: If A:B = 3:4 and B:C = 8:9, what is A:C?

lessons.title: Averages
lessons.description: Mean values and equal distribution.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Average = Sum of all observations / Number of observations.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Required for data interpretation and statistical word problems.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: If the average of N items is A, their total sum is N*A. If a new item is added, New Sum = N*A + New Item.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Calculate total sums to solve complex average transitions.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: Average of 4 numbers is 10. Sum = 40. A 5th number (20) is added. New sum = 60. New average = 60/5 = 12.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: If all numbers in a set increase by X, the new average also increases by X.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Averaging two averages without weighting them by their group sizes.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: For weighted averages, use the formula: (N1*A1 + N2*A2) / (N1 + N2).

sections.question: The average age of 10 students is 15. If the teacher's age is included, the average becomes 16. What is the teacher's age?
sections.explanation: Sum of 10 students = 150. Sum of 11 people = 11 * 16 = 176. Teacher = 176 - 150 = 26.

lessons.title: Simple Interest
lessons.description: Linear interest calculation.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Simple Interest is calculated only on the principal amount for the entire period.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Direct formula application; frequently tested in banking and IT services exams.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: SI = (P * R * T) / 100, where P = Principal, R = Rate %, T = Time.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Plug values into the formula. Ensure T is in years if R is per annum.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: If a sum doubles in T years, the interest earned equals the principal. So (P*R*T)/100 = P => R*T = 100.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Using months instead of years for T without dividing by 12.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: In SI, the interest earned each year is constant.

sections.question: A sum of money doubles itself in 10 years at simple interest. What is the rate of interest?
sections.explanation: Interest = Principal. So P = P*R*10/100. 1 = R/10. R = 10%.

lessons.title: Compound Interest
lessons.description: Interest on interest.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Compound Interest is calculated on the principal and the accumulated interest of previous periods.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Tests calculation speed and understanding of exponential growth.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Amount = P(1 + R/100)^N. CI = Amount - Principal.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Use the formula, or use successive percentage changes for 2 or 3 years.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: For 2 years, effective CI rate = 2R + (R^2)/100. (e.g., for 10%, 20 + 1 = 21%).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Applying SI formula multiple times instead of CI formula.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Difference between CI and SI for 2 years = P * (R/100)^2.

sections.question: What is the effective compound interest rate for 2 years at 10% per annum?
sections.explanation: Using successive change: 10 + 10 + (10*10)/100 = 21%.

modules.title: Time Based Problems
modules.description: Work, speed, and relative motion.

lessons.title: Time and Work
lessons.description: Rates of completing tasks.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Time and Work deals with individuals completing a piece of work at different efficiencies.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: A classic placement topic (TCS Ninja, Wipro).

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: If a person does a job in X days, their 1-day work is 1/X.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Use the LCM method: assume Total Work = LCM of given days, then find daily efficiency.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: A takes 10 days. B takes 15 days. Total work = LCM(10,15) = 30 units. A's efficiency = 3 u/day. B's = 2 u/day. Together = 5 u/day. Time = 30/5 = 6 days.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: LCM method completely eliminates fractions and speeds up calculation by 3x.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Adding days instead of adding efficiencies.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Efficiency is inversely proportional to time taken.

sections.question: A can do a job in 20 days and B in 30 days. How long will they take working together?
sections.explanation: Work = LCM(20,30) = 60. A=3, B=2. Total efficiency = 5. Time = 60/5 = 12 days.

lessons.title: Pipes and Cisterns
lessons.description: Filling and emptying tanks.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Similar to Time and Work, but introduces negative efficiency (emptying pipes).

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Direct extension of work concepts.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Inlet pipe = positive work (+). Outlet pipe = negative work (-).

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Use the LCM method. Assign negative efficiency to the emptying pipe.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: Pipe A fills in 10h (+). Pipe B empties in 15h (-). LCM = 30 units. A = +3. B = -2. Net = +1 unit/hr. Time to fill = 30/1 = 30 hrs.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: The negative efficiency trick makes these problems identical to standard Time & Work.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Forgetting to subtract the efficiency of the outlet pipe.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: If net efficiency is negative, the tank will eventually empty, not fill.

sections.question: Pipe A fills a tank in 4 hours. Pipe B empties it in 6 hours. If both are opened, how long to fill?

lessons.title: Time, Speed and Distance
lessons.description: Motion and kinematics.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Deals with objects moving at constant speeds over distances.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Core physics concept applied to aptitude.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Distance = Speed * Time.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Ensure all units match (km/h vs m/s) before applying the formula.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: Speed = 72 km/h. Distance = 200m. Convert speed: 72 * 5/18 = 20 m/s. Time = 200/20 = 10 seconds.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: To convert km/h to m/s, multiply by 5/18. From m/s to km/h, multiply by 18/5.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Mixing km/h with seconds in calculations.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Average speed = Total Distance / Total Time. It is NOT the simple average of two speeds.

sections.question: Convert 90 km/h into m/s.

lessons.title: Boats and Streams
lessons.description: Relative speed in fluid.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Calculates speed of objects moving with or against a flowing current.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Requires understanding of relative motion.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Downstream speed (D) = Boat Speed (B) + Stream Speed (S). Upstream (U) = B - S.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Use the equations to solve for B or S: B = (D+U)/2, S = (D-U)/2.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: Boat speed = 10, Stream = 2. Downstream = 12. Upstream = 8.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Always remember: B = (D+U)/2 and S = (D-U)/2.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Confusing downstream (faster) with upstream (slower).

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: The boat's speed in still water is always exactly halfway between upstream and downstream speeds.

sections.question: A boat travels downstream at 14 km/h and upstream at 10 km/h. What is the speed of the stream?

lessons.title: Trains
lessons.description: Moving bodies with significant length.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Train problems require adding the length of the train to the distance covered.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: High frequency topic in TCS and Infosys.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: When a train passes a pole, Distance = Train Length. When it passes a platform, Distance = Train Length + Platform Length.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Relative speed: Add speeds if moving opposite, subtract if moving same direction.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: Train (100m) passes platform (150m). Total distance = 250m. If speed is 25m/s, time = 250/25 = 10s.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Always draw a quick mental picture to see if lengths should be added.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Forgetting to add the length of the platform to the distance.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: When two trains pass each other, you ALWAYS add their lengths, regardless of direction.

sections.question: A 200m train running at 20 m/s passes a pole. How long does it take?
sections.explanation: Distance = Train length = 200m. Time = 200 / 20 = 10s.

modules.title: Algebra
modules.description: Equations and identities.

lessons.title: Basic Algebra
lessons.description: Variables and expressions.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Algebra involves solving for unknown variables using mathematical expressions.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Foundational for solving word problems.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Use BODMAS/PEMDAS. Group like terms.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Translate word problems into equations (e.g. 'twice a number' -> 2x).

sections.title: Example
sections.content: If 3x + 5 = 20, then 3x = 15, so x = 5.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Plug the answer options into the equation instead of solving it algebraically to save time.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Making sign errors when moving terms across the equals sign.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Back-substitution from options is often faster than solving the equation.

sections.question: If 4x - 7 = 13, what is x?

lessons.title: Linear Equations
lessons.description: Equations with degree 1.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Simultaneous equations involving two or more variables.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Used in age problems and mixing problems.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Use substitution or elimination methods.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Multiply one equation by a constant to eliminate a variable when added.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Add or subtract the equations entirely to quickly find x+y or x-y if asked.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Solving for the wrong variable.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: In age problems, if a ratio is given for '5 years ago', apply the -5 to both ages.

sections.question: If x + y = 12 and x - y = 4, what is x * y?
sections.explanation: Adding gives 2x = 16 -> x = 8. Subtracting gives 2y = 8 -> y = 4. 8 * 4 = 32.

lessons.title: Quadratic Equations
lessons.description: Equations with degree 2.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Equations in the form ax^2 + bx + c = 0.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Commonly appears in advanced aptitude tests.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Roots formula: x = [-b +/- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)] / 2a. Sum of roots = -b/a. Product = c/a.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Factorize by splitting the middle term.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0. Factors of 6 that add to -5 are -2, -3. Roots are 2 and 3.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Change the sign of the split terms to get the roots directly (if a=1).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Forgetting the +/- in the quadratic formula.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: If the discriminant (b^2 - 4ac) is negative, the roots are imaginary.

sections.question: What is the sum of the roots of 2x^2 - 8x + 5 = 0?
sections.explanation: Sum of roots = -b/a = -(-8)/2 = 4.

lessons.title: Algebraic Identities
lessons.description: Standard algebraic formulas.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Identities are equations that hold true for all values of the variables.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Crucial for simplifying complex polynomial expressions.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Recognize the pattern in the question and apply the identity.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: If x + 1/x = k, then x^2 + 1/x^2 = k^2 - 2.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Expanding binomials manually instead of using identities.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Memorize the identity a^3 + b^3 = (a+b)(a^2 - ab + b^2).

sections.question: If x + 1/x = 3, what is x^2 + 1/x^2?

lessons.title: Progressions
lessons.description: Arithmetic and Geometric sequences.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: AP has a common difference. GP has a common ratio.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Often asked in logical reasoning as well as quant.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: AP nth term: a + (n-1)d. AP Sum: n/2 * (2a + (n-1)d). GP nth term: a*r^(n-1).

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Identify 'a' (first term) and 'd' or 'r'. Plug into formula.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: Find 10th term of AP: 2, 5, 8... a=2, d=3. Term = 2 + 9*3 = 29.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Sum of first N natural numbers = N(N+1)/2.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Using AP formulas on a GP sequence.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: If 3 terms are in AP, let them be a-d, a, a+d.

sections.question: What is the sum of the first 100 natural numbers?

modules.title: Advanced Aptitude
modules.description: Combinatorics, probability, and geometry.

lessons.title: Permutations
lessons.description: Arranging objects.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Permutation is the number of ways to ARRANGE objects where order matters.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Used in seating arrangement and word-building problems.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: nPr = n! / (n-r)!. Arrangement of n distinct objects = n!.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Identify if order matters. If it does, use permutations.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: Ways to arrange A, B, C = 3! = 6.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: If some items are identical, divide by the factorial of their counts (e.g., APPLE = 5! / 2!).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Using permutation when order doesn't matter (combination).

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Arranging n people in a circle = (n-1)! ways.

sections.question: In how many ways can the letters of the word MATH be arranged?
sections.explanation: 4 distinct letters. 4! = 4*3*2*1 = 24.

lessons.title: Combinations
lessons.description: Selecting objects.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Combination is the number of ways to SELECT objects where order does NOT matter.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Used in forming committees, picking cards, or balls from a bag.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Identify if it's purely a selection. Use nCr.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: Select 2 people from 5. 5C2 = (5*4)/(2*1) = 10.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: nCr = nC(n-r). E.g., 100C98 is just 100C2.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Multiplying instead of adding for 'OR' conditions.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: 'AND' means multiply. 'OR' means add.

sections.question: How many ways can you select a committee of 3 from 6 people?

lessons.title: Probability
lessons.description: Chances of an event occurring.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Probability = Favorable Outcomes / Total Outcomes.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Very common in product company interviews.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: P(E) = n(E) / n(S). Total probability = 1.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Find total outcomes (sample space). Then find favorable outcomes using combinations.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: Roll a die. P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: If events are independent, P(A and B) = P(A) * P(B).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Calculating combinations incorrectly when pulling multiple items.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Probability can never be greater than 1.

sections.question: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue balls. Probability of drawing a blue ball?
sections.explanation: Favorable = 2. Total = 5. P = 2/5.

lessons.title: Geometry
lessons.description: Lines, angles, and shapes.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Properties of 2D shapes, angles, and triangles.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Required for spatial reasoning.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Sum of angles in a triangle = 180. Pythagoras: a^2 + b^2 = c^2.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Draw the figure. Apply basic properties.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: Triangle with sides 3, 4, 5 is a right triangle because 3^2 + 4^2 = 5^2.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Recognize Pythagorean triplets (3-4-5, 5-12-13).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Assuming a triangle is right-angled without proof.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: The sum of any two sides of a triangle must be greater than the third side.

sections.question: What is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with sides 6 and 8?

lessons.title: Mensuration
lessons.description: Area and Volume.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Calculation of area (2D) and volume (3D) of shapes.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Direct formula application.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Area of circle = pi*r^2. Volume of cylinder = pi*r^2*h.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Memorize formulas and plug in values.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: Area of square with side 4 = 16.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: If radius of a circle doubles, area becomes 4 times.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Mixing up formulas for surface area and volume.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Units matter. Area is square units, volume is cubic.

sections.question: What is the area of a circle with radius 7? (Use pi=22/7)

lessons.title: Data Interpretation
lessons.description: Extracting info from graphs.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Analyzing bar charts, pie charts, and tables to answer questions.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Core skill for consulting and data roles.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Involves fast calculation of percentages and ratios from visual data.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Do not calculate exact values if approximations suffice.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: If A is 480 and B is 950, A is roughly 50% of B.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Read the axes and legends carefully before looking at the questions.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Calculating everything to 2 decimal places when options are far apart.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: DI tests calculation speed. Use fraction shortcuts.

sections.question: If a pie chart segment is 90 degrees, what percentage of the total does it represent?

title: Logical Reasoning
description: Develop structured reasoning and problem-solving skills for placement examinations.

modules.title: Patterns
modules.description: Identify numerical and alphabetical sequences.

lessons.title: Number Series
lessons.description: Identifying the hidden mathematical sequence.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: A number series is a sequence of numbers following a specific mathematical rule.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: This is the most common reasoning question across all aptitude tests.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Identify the gap (difference) between consecutive numbers. If the gap increases rapidly, it's multiplication/squares. If it increases slowly, it's addition.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Calculate the difference between adjacent terms. If no pattern emerges, calculate the difference of the differences (double difference).

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
Series: 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, ?
Differences: 3, 5, 7, 9. The next difference is 11. So 26 + 11 = 37.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Check for n^2 + 1, n^2 - 1, n^3 patterns immediately if the numbers look familiar.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Adding incorrectly during stressful timed tests.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: If the series alternately increases and decreases, it might be two intertwined series.

sections.question: Find the next number: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ?
sections.explanation: These are perfect squares (1^2, 2^2, 3^2, etc.). 6^2 = 36.

lessons.title: Alphabet Series
lessons.description: Patterns using letters.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: A series where letters are arranged according to a specific logic.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Tests your speed in mapping letters to their positional values.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: A=1, B=2 ... Z=26. Also reverse order Z=1 ... A=26.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Convert the letters to their numerical positions and solve it like a Number Series.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
Series: A, C, F, J, O, ?
Positions: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15.
Differences: +2, +3, +4, +5. Next difference is +6. 15 + 6 = 21, which is U.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Memorize EJOTY (5, 10, 15, 20, 25) to quickly find positions of nearby letters.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Counting on fingers instead of memorizing positional values.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Write down the alphabet with numbers 1-26 before the exam begins on your scratchpad.

sections.question: Find the next letter: B, E, H, K, ?
sections.explanation: Positions: 2, 5, 8, 11. Difference is +3. 11+3 = 14 = N.

lessons.title: Alphanumeric Series
lessons.description: Combining letters and numbers.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: A sequence containing both letters and digits.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Often used to increase the visual complexity of simple patterns.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Treat the letters and numbers as two separate, independent series.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Solve the number pattern first, then the letter pattern, and combine them.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
Series: A1, C4, E9, G16, ?
Letters: A, C, E, G (+2) -> I
Numbers: 1, 4, 9, 16 (squares) -> 25
Answer: I25

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Don't try to link the letter to the number unless they are clearly tied (e.g., A1, B2).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Getting overwhelmed by the combination and missing simple individual patterns.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Focus on one element type across the series first.

sections.question: Find the next term: 2Z5, 7Y7, 14X9, 23W11, 34V13, ?

lessons.title: Analogies
lessons.description: Finding proportional relationships.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: A comparison between two things, typically on the basis of their structure.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Tests vocabulary, general knowledge, and logic simultaneously.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: A : B :: C : D. The relationship between A and B is identical to C and D.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Form a sentence that describes the relationship between A and B. Apply that exact sentence to C.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
OVEN : BAKE :: KNIFE : ?
Sentence: An OVEN is a tool used to BAKE.
A KNIFE is a tool used to CUT.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Read all options before deciding; sometimes multiple fit loosely, but one fits perfectly.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Picking an option related to C, but not exhibiting the same relationship.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Check the part of speech (noun, verb, adjective) to eliminate wrong answers.

sections.question: Tree : Forest :: Soldier : ?
sections.explanation: A collection of Trees makes a Forest. A collection of Soldiers makes an Army.

lessons.title: Odd One Out
lessons.description: Classification and finding the anomaly.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Selecting the item that does not belong to the given group.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Tests your ability to find a common rule that applies to all but one.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Find the underlying category (e.g., primes, capitals, synonyms) that links the majority.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Look for squares, primes, or divisibility for numbers. Look for vowels, consonants, or alphabetical gaps for letters.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: Options: 16, 25, 36, 50. All are perfect squares except 50.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: For numbers, always check prime numbers and perfect squares first.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Finding a rule for the odd one instead of finding the rule for the group.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: The 'Odd One' is odd because the OTHERS share a property, not just because it is unique.

sections.question: Find the odd one out: Apple, Orange, Banana, Carrot
sections.explanation: Apple, Orange, and Banana are fruits. Carrot is a vegetable.

modules.title: Basic Reasoning
modules.description: Coding, relations, and directions.

lessons.title: Coding-Decoding
lessons.description: Encrypting and decrypting information.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: A process of converting a word to a code and vice-versa using a specific rule.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Heavily tested in mass recruiter exams.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Identify the shift (+1, -2, reverse order) applied to each letter.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Write the word and the code directly below it. Map the changes column by column.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: If APPLE is coded as BQQMF (each letter +1), then ORANGE is coded as PSBOHF.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Look for diagonal coding (first letter shifts and becomes the last letter).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Assuming a constant shift when the shift is increasing (+1, +2, +3).

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Always write the positional values above the letters if the pattern isn't obvious.

sections.question: If CAT is coded as 24, what is DOG coded as?

lessons.title: Blood Relations
lessons.description: Family trees and connections.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Tracing family relationships through generations.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Tests your ability to map complex relational logic.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Use a family tree diagram. Squares for males, circles for females. Vertical lines for generations, horizontal for siblings/spouses.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Break the statement down from the end to the beginning (e.g., 'My father's only son' -> me/my brother).

sections.title: Example
sections.content: 'A is the brother of B's father.' Diagram: B is at bottom. Father above B. A next to Father. A is B's uncle.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Assume 'My' refers to the speaker. Work backward from 'My'.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Assuming gender based on names (e.g., assuming 'Pat' is male/female).

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Never assume gender by name in logical reasoning unless explicitly stated.

sections.question: Pointing to a photograph, a man says 'She is the mother of my son's wife's daughter'. How is she related to the man?
sections.explanation: Son's wife's daughter = Son's daughter = Granddaughter. Mother of granddaughter = Son's wife = Daughter-in-law.

lessons.title: Direction Sense
lessons.description: Navigating 2D space.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Tracing the path and finding final position/distance relative to the start.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Combines logic with basic geometry (Pythagoras).

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: North (Up), South (Down), East (Right), West (Left).

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Draw a map step-by-step as you read the problem. Mark distances.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: Walk 3m East, turn left (North) walk 4m. Distance from start = sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = 5m.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Imagine yourself facing the direction of travel to correctly identify left and right turns.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Confusing East and West on the paper.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Always draw a small compass (N, S, E, W) on the corner of your scratchpad.

sections.question: A man walks 5km South, turns right and walks 3km. Then he turns right and walks 5km. What direction is he from the start?
sections.explanation: South (down 5), right (West 3), right (North 5). He is 3km directly West of the start.

lessons.title: Ranking and Ordering
lessons.description: Positions in a queue.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Finding the total number of people or someone's rank from the other end.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Requires careful boundary management (inclusive/exclusive counting).

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Total = (Rank from Left) + (Rank from Right) - 1.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Draw a line and mark the positions. Apply the formula.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: A is 10th from left and 15th from right. Total = 10 + 15 - 1 = 24.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Subtract 1 because the person is counted twice.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Forgetting to subtract 1 in the total formula.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: If A and B swap positions, track the empty 'seats', not just the people.

sections.question: In a class of 40 students, Rohan's rank is 15th from top. What is his rank from the bottom?
sections.explanation: Total = Top + Bottom - 1. 40 = 15 + Bottom - 1. Bottom = 40 - 14 = 26.

lessons.title: Clocks and Calendars
lessons.description: Time-based logical math.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Finding angles between clock hands or determining the day of the week.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Frequently asked in core placement tests.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Minute hand moves 6 deg/min. Hour hand moves 0.5 deg/min. Angle = |30*H - 5.5*M|.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: For calendars, find 'odd days' (remainder when dividing total days by 7).

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: A normal year has 1 odd day. A leap year has 2 odd days.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Forgetting that the hour hand moves while the minute hand moves.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Every 400 years has 0 odd days. This resets the calendar math completely.

sections.question: What is the angle between the hands of a clock at 4:20?

modules.title: Advanced Reasoning
modules.description: Syllogisms, data sufficiency, and puzzles.

lessons.title: Syllogisms
lessons.description: Deductive logic and Venn diagrams.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Determining if conclusions logically follow from given statements.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Tests strict logical deduction without real-world assumptions.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Draw Venn diagrams to represent 'All', 'Some', 'No', and 'Some Not'.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Draw the basic diagram. A conclusion must be true in ALL possible valid diagrams to follow.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
Statements: All Cats are Dogs. Some Dogs are Birds. 
Conclusion: Some Cats are Birds. (False - possible, but not definite).

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: If a statement is positive, negative definite conclusions usually do not follow.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Bringing real-world knowledge into the problem (e.g., 'cats aren't dogs').

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Only accept a conclusion if it is 100% true based ONLY on the statements provided.

sections.question: Statements: All A are B. All B are C. Conclusion: All A are C.
sections.explanation: If A is entirely inside B, and B is entirely inside C, then A is entirely inside C.

lessons.title: Statements and Conclusions
lessons.description: Analyzing logical implications.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Evaluating whether a conclusion can be safely drawn from a real-world statement.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Used to test critical reasoning.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: The conclusion must be directly related and logically derived from the statement.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Read the statement carefully. Do not assume any external facts.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: Statement: The company is hiring only experienced candidates. Conclusion: The company wants to reduce training time. (Valid assumption).

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Avoid conclusions that use extreme words like 'always', 'never', 'only' unless the statement implies it.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Making assumptions that go too far beyond the provided text.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: If the conclusion requires two leaps of logic, it is usually invalid.

sections.question: Statement: A diet rich in fruits prevents diseases. Conclusion: Everyone should eat fruits.
sections.explanation: Since it prevents diseases, it is a logical recommendation for everyone.

lessons.title: Data Sufficiency
lessons.description: Evaluating information completeness.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Determining if the provided statements are enough to answer the question.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Saves time because you don't actually have to solve the problem.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Check Statement 1 alone. Then Statement 2 alone. If both fail, combine them.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Do NOT calculate the exact answer. Just verify if a unique answer exists.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
Q: What is x? 
S1: x + y = 10 
S2: x - y = 4 
Result: Both together are sufficient.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Once you know the statements are sufficient, STOP calculating.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Solving the entire math problem unnecessarily, wasting 3 minutes.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Always test Statement 2 alone and pretend Statement 1 does not exist.

sections.question:
What is the value of x? 
I: x^2 = 25 
II: x > 0
sections.explanation: I gives x = 5 or -5. II gives x > 0. Together, we know exactly that x = 5.

lessons.title: Seating Arrangement
lessons.description: Logical spatial positioning.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Placing individuals in a row or circle based on a set of rules.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Common in banking exams and advanced IT placements.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Identify fixed information first. Draw the circle/row. Fill in relative information.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Start with the most definite statement (e.g., 'A sits perfectly opposite B').

sections.title: Example
sections.content: If 'A is second to the left of B', place B first, then count two seats left to place A.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: For circular arrangements, always be clear if they are facing the center or outside.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Placing an uncertain variable immediately and getting stuck later.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Write down all conditions in short notation before drawing the diagram.

sections.question: A, B, C, D sit in a circle facing the center. A is opposite C. B is to the immediate right of A. Who is opposite B?
sections.explanation: Draw it. A is Top, C is Bottom. Right of A is B (Right side). So D must be on the Left side, opposite B.

title: Verbal Ability
description: Improve grammar, vocabulary, comprehension, and sentence-solving skills for placement tests.

modules.title: Vocabulary
modules.description: Synonyms, antonyms, and substitutions.

lessons.title: Synonyms
lessons.description: Words with similar meanings.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: A synonym is a word or phrase that means exactly or nearly the same as another.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Tests your English lexicon, crucial for communication roles.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Identify the root, prefix, and suffix of the word if you don't know the exact meaning.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Read the word in context if a sentence is provided. Substitute the options to see which fits best.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
'The manager was ASTOUNDED by the results.' 
Options: Amazed, Angry, Bored. 
'Amazed' fits the context perfectly.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Use the elimination method based on the positive or negative tone of the word.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Picking an antonym by mistake because it is a closely associated word.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Learn 10 new words daily leading up to the placement season.

sections.question: What is the synonym of 'Abundant'?
sections.explanation: Abundant means existing or available in large quantities; plentiful.

lessons.title: Antonyms
lessons.description: Words with opposite meanings.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: An antonym is a word opposite in meaning to another.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Tests precise understanding of word nuances.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Identify the core meaning and tone (positive/negative) of the given word.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Find a word in the options that has the exact opposite tone and scale.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: Antonym of 'Optimistic'. Optimistic is positive (hopeful). We need a negative word. 'Pessimistic' is the exact opposite.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Prefixes like un-, in-, dis-, im- often form antonyms (e.g., capable -> incapable).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Picking a synonym by mistake, as test makers always include the synonym as option A.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Always double-check the question header (Synonym vs Antonym) before clicking.

sections.question: What is the antonym of 'Transparent'?
sections.explanation: Transparent allows light through; opaque blocks it entirely.

lessons.title: One-Word Substitution
lessons.description: Replacing a phrase with a single word.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Using one specific word to describe a lengthy phrase or sentence.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Reduces wordiness and tests advanced vocabulary.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Understand the definition provided and map it to standard English nouns/adjectives.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Look for root words. For example, 'cide' means killing (homicide), 'ology' means study of (biology).

sections.title: Example
sections.content: 'A person who hates mankind' -> Misanthrope. (Misan = hate, anthrope = mankind).

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Learn common roots (phobia, cracy, cide, logy, phil) to guess words you haven't seen.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Guessing a word that sounds similar but means something else.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Group words by roots when studying to memorize them 10x faster.

sections.question: What is the one-word substitution for 'A life history written by oneself'?
sections.explanation: Auto = self. Bio = life. Graphy = writing.

lessons.title: Vocabulary in Context
lessons.description: Deducing meaning from a sentence.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Finding the meaning of a word based on how it is used in a specific sentence.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Tests practical English usage rather than rote memorization.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Look at the surrounding words (context clues) to deduce the tone and meaning.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Blank out the target word, guess a simple word that fits, and find the closest match in the options.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: 'His ERUDITE speech impressed the scholars.' -> The speech impressed scholars, so it must mean 'educated' or 'learned'.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Conjunctions like 'but' or 'although' indicate a shift in tone. 'And' indicates a continuation.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Ignoring the sentence and choosing the most common definition of the word.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Some words have multiple meanings; always rely on the sentence context.

sections.question: In the sentence 'The water was so MURKY we couldn't see the bottom', what does MURKY mean?
sections.explanation: Since they couldn't see the bottom, the water must be unclear or dark.

modules.title: Grammar
modules.description: Rules of English structure.

lessons.title: Parts of Speech
lessons.description: Nouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: The categories into which words are classified according to their functions in sentences.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Forms the foundation for sentence correction questions.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Identify the role of the word. Is it an action (verb), a thing (noun), or descriptive (adjective/adverb)?

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Analyze the sentence structure (Subject-Verb-Object).

sections.title: Example
sections.content: 'He runs quickly.' He=Pronoun, runs=Verb, quickly=Adverb.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs. Adjectives modify nouns.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Confusing adjectives (good) with adverbs (well).

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Understand the function, not just the word. 'Water' can be a noun (drink water) or a verb (water the plants).

sections.question: Identify the adverb in: 'The dog barked loudly.'
sections.explanation: 'Loudly' modifies the verb 'barked'.

lessons.title: Subject-Verb Agreement
lessons.description: Matching subjects to their verbs.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: A singular subject takes a singular verb, and a plural subject takes a plural verb.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: The #1 most tested grammar rule in placement exams.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Identify the true subject of the sentence, ignoring any prepositional phrases in between.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Match the verb explicitly to the true subject.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: 'The box of chocolates IS on the table.' (Subject is 'box', not 'chocolates').

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Words like 'Everyone', 'Each', 'Anyone' always take a singular verb.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Matching the verb to the noun closest to it, rather than the actual subject.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: When two subjects are joined by 'or'/'nor', the verb agrees with the subject closest to it.

sections.question: Which sentence is correct?
options: The group of boys are playing.
The group of boys is playing.
The group of boys were playing.
sections.explanation: The subject is 'group' (singular), so the verb must be 'is'.

lessons.title: Tenses
lessons.description: Time of action.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Verb forms that indicate the time (past, present, future) of an action.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Crucial for paragraph coherence and error detection.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Ensure the tense is consistent throughout the sentence unless a time shift is explicitly stated.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Look for time markers (e.g., 'yesterday', 'since 2010', 'tomorrow').

sections.title: Example
sections.content: 'I have been living here since 2010.' (Present Perfect Continuous - started in past, continuing now).

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Use 'had + V3' (Past Perfect) when two past actions occur, to show which happened first.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Mixing past and present tenses in the same clause incorrectly.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: The Past Perfect tense ('had done') requires another past action to anchor it.

sections.question: Complete the sentence: 'By the time we arrived, the train _______.'
sections.explanation: Two past actions. The train leaving happened first, so it takes the past perfect ('had left').

lessons.title: Sentence Correction
lessons.description: Fixing grammatical errors.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Identifying and correcting errors in a given sentence.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: A staple of TCS, Infosys, and Wipro verbal sections.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Check S-V agreement, tenses, pronouns, idioms, and parallel structure.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Read the sentence carefully. Identify the underlined portion and test each option.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: 'He is more taller than me.' -> 'He is taller than I.' (Double comparative is wrong, and subject pronoun is needed).

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Shorter answers are usually better if grammatically correct (avoid wordiness).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Selecting an option that changes the original meaning of the sentence.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Check for parallelism: 'I like hiking, swimming, and to bike' -> '...and biking'.

sections.question: Correct the sentence: 'Neither of the answers are correct.'
options: Neither of the answers is correct.
sections.explanation: 'Neither' is a singular subject and requires the singular verb 'is'.

modules.title: Comprehension
modules.description: Reading and understanding passages.

lessons.title: Reading Comprehension
lessons.description: Extracting information from text.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Reading a passage and answering questions based on it.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Tests reading speed, retention, and analytical ability.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Identify the main idea, tone of the author, and specific facts.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Read the questions FIRST, then skim the passage for keywords.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: If a question asks for the 'Main Idea', look at the first and last paragraphs.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Do not infer beyond what is stated or strongly implied in the text.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Using outside knowledge to answer a question instead of the passage.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: The answer is ALWAYS in the text, either explicitly or implicitly.

sections.question: If a passage discusses the negative impacts of pollution, what is the likely tone of the author?
sections.explanation: Discussing negative impacts naturally implies a concerned or critical tone.

lessons.title: Para Jumbles
lessons.description: Reordering sentences.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: A set of jumbled sentences that need to be arranged into a coherent paragraph.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Tests logical flow and understanding of transitions.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Identify the opening sentence (usually introduces a noun or concept). Look for links (pronouns, conjunctions).

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Find mandatory pairs (e.g., Sentence A introduces 'John', Sentence B says 'He did this'. A must precede B).

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
Sentences: 
P. But he failed. 
Q. John tried hard. 
R. He decided to quit.
Order: Q -> P -> R.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Look for transition words like 'However', 'Therefore', 'Also' to connect ideas.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Trying to read all possible combinations instead of finding mandatory pairs.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Use the multiple-choice options to eliminate invalid starting sentences quickly.

sections.question: Arrange: P: Finally, he succeeded. Q: He started a business. R: It struggled at first.
sections.explanation: Q introduces the action. R describes the initial state. P concludes.

lessons.title: Fill in the Blanks
lessons.description: Completing the sentence logically.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Choosing the correct word to complete a sentence.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Tests vocabulary and context simultaneously.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Analyze the tone (positive/negative) and the grammar required (noun/verb).

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Predict a word that fits before looking at the options.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: 'The CEO was known for his _____, always giving money to charity.' -> Prediction: Generosity. Matches option: Philanthropy.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Pay attention to prepositional phrases that follow the blank.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Picking a word that sounds good but violates grammatical rules.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: If there are two blanks, one word usually eliminates 2-3 options instantly.

sections.question: Despite his _______ wealth, he lived a very simple life.
sections.explanation: 'Despite' implies a contrast. Living simple contrasts with having 'immense' wealth.

title: Data Interpretation
description: Learn to analyze tables, charts, graphs, and numerical datasets under time pressure.

modules.title: Basic DI
modules.description: Foundations of reading and comparing tabular data.

lessons.title: Reading Tables
lessons.description: Extracting data from rows and columns.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Tabular DI involves data presented in a grid format with rows and columns.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Tables are the most common and data-dense format in DI.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Identify the headers, units (thousands, percentages), and any footnotes before reading the numbers.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Use approximation for large numbers (e.g., 4987/10012 is approximately 5000/10000 = 50%).

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Learn fraction to percentage values to calculate growth rates mentally.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Calculating exact values when options are widely spaced.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Always scan the options first. If they are far apart (e.g., 10%, 25%, 50%), use heavy approximation.

sections.question: If revenue increases from 200 to 250, what is the percentage increase?

lessons.title: Data Comparison
lessons.description: Comparing quantities quickly.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Comparing fractions or ratios derived from a table without fully calculating them.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Saves massive amounts of time during calculations.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Cross-multiply fractions to compare them: a/b vs c/d -> compare ad vs bc.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Use the cross-multiplication trick or convert to rough percentages.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: Compare 4/9 and 5/11. 4*11=44, 9*5=45. So 5/11 is greater.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: If the numerator increases and the denominator decreases, the fraction value strictly increases.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Doing long division to compare fractions.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Look at the percentage growth of the numerator vs denominator to compare ratios.

sections.question: Which fraction is larger: 7/15 or 8/17?

modules.title: Graphs
modules.description: Visual data interpretation.

lessons.title: Bar Graphs
lessons.description: Comparing heights.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Data represented using rectangular bars where height is proportional to value.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Very common for comparing multiple companies or years.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Read the scale carefully (e.g., each line represents 10 units).

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Use visual approximation before doing math. You can often see which year had highest growth just by looking.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: Bar A is height 40, Bar B is 50. B is 25% larger than A.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Use the edge of your rough paper or an on-screen straight line to compare heights if numbers aren't explicitly written.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Misreading the scale (e.g., reading 45 as 40).

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Pay attention to whether the bars are stacked or clustered.

sections.question: If a bar graph scale has 0 at the bottom and 100 at the top with 4 lines in between, what does each line represent?
sections.explanation: 5 intervals (0 to 100). 100 / 5 = 20 per line.

lessons.title: Line Graphs
lessons.description: Tracking trends over time.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Data points connected by straight line segments, usually showing change over time.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Excellent for showing percentage growth or decline.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: The steepness of the line indicates the rate of change.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Focus on the 'nodes' (data points). Calculate the difference between nodes.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: Line goes from (2018, 100) to (2019, 150). Growth = 50%.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: A horizontal line means 0% growth (constant value).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Confusing a steep line with high absolute value (it only means high growth rate).

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: When two lines cross, their values are equal at that specific point in time.

sections.question: A line graph goes from 50 in Jan to 50 in Feb. What is the growth rate?
sections.explanation: Value remained the same, so growth is 0%.

lessons.title: Pie Charts
lessons.description: Parts of a whole.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: A circular chart divided into sectors, illustrating numerical proportion.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Used heavily to show market share or budget allocation.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Total circle = 360 degrees or 100%.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: 1% = 3.6 degrees. To convert % to degrees, multiply by 3.6.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: Sector is 20%. Angle = 20 * 3.6 = 72 degrees.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: If the total value is a multiple of 100 (e.g., 5000), 1% is 50. Just multiply percentages by 50.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Calculating the exact value for each sector when asked for a ratio between two sectors.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: If asked for the ratio of two slices, just take the ratio of their percentages/angles. Do not calculate absolute values.

sections.question: If a slice is 90 degrees, what fraction of the total does it represent?

modules.title: Advanced DI
modules.description: Complex and mixed data.

lessons.title: Mixed Graphs
lessons.description: Combining multiple data sources.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Problems featuring a combination of a pie chart and a table, or a bar and line graph.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Tests your ability to cross-reference data under pressure.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Understand how the two graphs are linked (e.g., Pie chart shows Total Students, Table shows Male:Female ratio).

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Derive the base value from the first graph, then apply the second graph's metric.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: Total = 1000 (from pie chart slice of 10%). Male:Female = 3:2 (from table). Males = (3/5)*1000 = 600.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Create a master table on your scratchpad for the values you calculate, as they are often reused in subsequent questions.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Reading data from the wrong graph or applying a ratio to the total instead of the slice.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Link the datasets in your mind before answering the first question.

sections.question: Graph A says total cars = 100. Graph B says 40% are red. How many red cars?

lessons.title: Caselet DI
lessons.description: Paragraph-based data.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Data provided in the form of a paragraph rather than a visual chart.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Requires you to construct your own table or Venn diagram.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Read the passage carefully and draw a table or a Venn diagram (if sets/intersections are involved).

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Fill in the explicit data first. Use variables (x, y) for unknown data and solve using given totals.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: 'Out of 100 people, 60 like tea, 50 like coffee. 20 like both.' -> Venn diagram setup.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Once your table/Venn diagram is complete, you can solve all 5 questions in 1 minute.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Trying to answer questions without drawing a table first.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Spend 3-4 minutes constructing the table. It is an investment that pays off instantly.

sections.question: In a class of 50, 30 play cricket, 25 play football, 10 play both. How many play neither?
sections.explanation: Total playing = n(C) + n(F) - n(C and F) = 30 + 25 - 10 = 45. Neither = 50 - 45 = 5.

lessons.title: Data Sufficiency (DI)
lessons.description: Checking if a graph is complete.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Determining if the provided data/graphs are enough to answer the question.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Often a trap where percentages are given but no absolute values.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: You cannot find an absolute value if only ratios or percentages are provided.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Check if a base value is provided in ANY of the statements.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: S1: A's salary is 20% more than B's. S2: B's salary increased by 10%. Question: What is A's salary? -> Neither is sufficient (no base value).

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Look out for missing variables. If a pie chart gives percentages but no total, absolute questions cannot be answered.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Assuming a total (like 100 or 1000) when it's not given.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: In DI Data Sufficiency, 90% of the time, the trap is a missing base value.

sections.question:
Is the data sufficient to find the number of boys? 
I: Ratio of boys to girls is 3:2. 
II: There are 20 more boys than girls.
sections.explanation: I gives ratio. II gives difference (3x - 2x = x = 20). Together we find boys = 3(20) = 60.

title: Placement Aptitude
description: Company-specific patterns, time management strategies, and test-taking techniques.

modules.title: Company Specific Patterns
modules.description: Understanding how different companies structure their tests.

lessons.title: TCS Ninja Patterns
lessons.description: TCS specific quantitative and reasoning focus.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: TCS Ninja focuses heavily on advanced quantitative aptitude (Time & Work, Profit & Loss) and data interpretation.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Knowing the pattern allows you to allocate study time to the highest-weightage topics.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Focus on LCM/HCF, Time & Work, Speed & Distance, and Basic DI. Use the on-screen calculator efficiently.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: TCS questions are often wordy. Read the last sentence first to know what to solve for.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: If a TCS question gives a 5-line story about two workers, jump to the end: 'Find the time taken by A alone.'

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Do not get stuck on 'Advanced Quant' questions; they carry the same marks as easy ones.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Spending 5 minutes on a difficult permutation question while missing 3 easy arithmetic questions.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: TCS Ninja does not usually have negative marking, so never leave a question blank.

sections.question: Which of these topics is historically a high-weightage area in TCS Ninja?
sections.explanation: TCS heavily favors core arithmetic like Time and Work.

lessons.title: Infosys Logical
lessons.description: Infosys specific reasoning focus.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Infosys is known for having a very challenging logical reasoning section.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: You must be fast at syllogisms, data sufficiency, and puzzles.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Practice Data Sufficiency and Syllogisms extensively. You must solve them in < 45 seconds.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: For Infosys, draw Venn diagrams immediately when reading the question.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: If you see a puzzle with 5 questions attached, invest 3-4 minutes solving the puzzle grid first.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Infosys often has sectional cutoffs. Do not ignore the verbal section.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Guessing blindly on Data Sufficiency.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: Data sufficiency in Infosys is a trap to make you solve the whole problem. Just check if it's solvable.

sections.question: What is the best approach for a 5-question puzzle block in Infosys?
sections.explanation: Mapping the puzzle first allows you to answer all 5 questions instantly.

modules.title: Test Strategies
modules.description: Time management and elimination.

lessons.title: Elimination Techniques
lessons.description: Removing wrong options.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Using logic, units, or estimation to eliminate 2-3 wrong options without fully solving the problem.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Saves critical minutes during a timed exam.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Check the unit digit of the calculation. Check if the answer should be positive/negative or integer/fraction.

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: If 123 * 456 is asked, the unit digit must be 3*6 = 18 -> ends in 8. Eliminate options not ending in 8.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: Q: Area of a circle with radius 7? Options: 153, 154, 155. Pi = 22/7. Area must be a multiple of 11. Only 154 is.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Always check divisibility rules (especially 3, 9, 11) against the options.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Solving the entire calculation before looking at the options.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: The options are part of the question. Use them to your advantage.

sections.question: What is 453 * 217?
sections.explanation: Unit digit is 3 * 7 = 21 -> ends in 1. Only 98301 ends in 1.

lessons.title: Skimming Questions
lessons.description: Finding the easy wins.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: Quickly scanning a test to solve the easiest 40% of questions first.

sections.title: Why it Matters
sections.content: Maximizes your score and builds confidence.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: Categorize questions visually into: Do Now (1 min), Do Later (2 mins), Skip (Too long).

sections.title: Standard Method
sections.content: Skip long reading comprehension passages or massive puzzles on your first pass.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: See a 6-line Time & Work problem? Skip it for round 2. See a basic Number Series? Do it now.

sections.title: Shortcut / Trick
sections.content: Your goal is to see every single question before the time runs out.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Ego-solving: refusing to skip a question because you 'should' know how to do it.

sections.title: Placement Tip
items: A hard question gives the exact same marks as an easy question.

sections.question: What should you do if you encounter a very long puzzle on question 1?
sections.explanation: Always secure easy marks first before tackling time-sinks.
